summary:
We developed ASTRA-SENTINEL, an AI-powered crew health monitoring system for astronauts. Its "AstroHealth AI" dashboard streams live vitals (heart rate, SpO2, temperature, blood pressure) and fuses them into a single risk level (Normal, Warning or Critical), with a plain-language reason for every alert. An on-board AstroHealth agent answers questions like "What should I do?" and suggests clear next steps.

It addresses the challenge directly. Astronauts face silent body changes in microgravity, communication delays of up to 22 minutes each way to Mars, and disconnected sensors whose warnings get missed. ASTRA-SENTINEL links the signals together, detects unusual trends early, explains its reasoning, and works offline so crews are not dependent on Earth. It is built with React, TypeScript, a Python API, Claude AI and NASA open data (OSDR, DONKI, FIRMS) for baselines and risk context. Prototype telemetry is simulated.

This matters because on long missions, help is minutes away at best, so crews need continuous, explainable, autonomous health monitoring to catch problems before they become emergencies, making deep-space missions safer.
details:
STRA-SENTINEL is a live crew health monitor for space missions. Sensors stream vitals (heart rate, SpO2, temperature, blood pressure) into a processing layer. An AI analysis stage then assigns a risk level of Normal, Warning or Critical, which appears on a Mission Control dashboard. The user journey has four steps: *Sense* (vitals stream in), *Detect* (AI spots unusual trends), *Explain* (plain-language reasons) and *Act* (alert and action plan). An AstroHealth agent lets astronauts ask "What should I do?" and get a clear plan back.

*Benefits*

•⁠ ⁠*Early warning:* it catches trends before symptoms appear.

•⁠ ⁠*Explainable:* every alert shows its reason, so crews and doctors can trust it.

•⁠ ⁠*Autonomous:* on-board AI works offline when Earth is up to 22 minutes away one way.

•⁠ ⁠*Connected:* it fuses signals that would otherwise be isolated warnings.

•⁠ ⁠*Low barrier:* it needs no flight hardware to build and test.

*Intended impact*

We want healthier astronauts and safer missions. As crews travel farther, they need to detect and respond to health problems themselves, without waiting for Mission Control. The same approach could also support remote and extreme-environment healthcare on Earth (my inference, not in the deck).

*Tools, languages and software*

•⁠ ⁠*Frontend:* React and TypeScript

•⁠ ⁠*Backend:* a Python API

•⁠ ⁠*AI:* Claude AI, plus an on-device agent for offline use

•⁠ ⁠*Data:* NASA open APIs: OSDR (astronaut studies OSD-379 and OSD-137 for healthy baselines), DONKI (solar storm alerts for radiation and spacewalk risk), FIRMS (active-fire data to calibrate cabin fire detection) and the NASA Image & Video Library (mission imagery)

•⁠ ⁠*Hardware:* none yet. Telemetry is simulated, and the roadmap is to connect real wearables.

*What makes it creative*

•⁠ ⁠It combines health monitoring, space weather and fire detection in one risk picture.

•⁠ ⁠It uses NASA open data for calibration, so there is no hardware dependency.

•⁠ ⁠It pairs an explainable alert system with a conversational agent that gives action plans, not just numbers.

•⁠ ⁠It is designed to run offline for deep space.

*Factors the team considered*

•⁠ ⁠*Communication delay:* the system must work without Earth.

•⁠ ⁠*Trust:* the AI has to explain itself.

•⁠ ⁠*Integration:* alerts should be linked, not siloed.

•⁠ ⁠*Honesty about limits:* the prototype uses simulated data.

•⁠ ⁠*Validation:* next steps are testing accuracy against OSDR studies and reviewing alerts with flight surgeons.

•⁠ ⁠*Real-world readiness:* connecting actual wearables is the final step.
